+This represents a typical workflow. Multiple jobs may be run simultaneously and logs may be monitored live or after the fact.
+
+#### Setup Server
+
+The setup server command is run as follows:
+
+```shell
+sudo hermione server setup
+```
+
+This command performs one-time setup and checking that is required to enable the server to run properly. Mostly, this sets up the required permissions in the cgroup file system.
+
+This program will assume that the cgroup of the current parent process or shell will be the one that the `hermione` server will be using.
+
+#### Run Server
+
+The run server command is run as follows:
+
+```shell
+hermione server run
+```
+
+This will start the server on port `:8443` listening on all available interfaces. All aspects of the service configuration are hard coded. The server will run and block until killed.
+
+This service runs the gRPC API described under the [API](#api) section and traffic is encrypted and protected by mTLS authentication.
+
+**Comments:**
+
+* _It would be nice if the server provided tooling for starting, stopping, checking status, and asking it to reload configuration, but these have been left off of the POC in the interest of time._
+* _Reading configuration from external files would also be best in a complete production system._
+
+#### Start Command
+
+```shell
+hermione start [options] <command-line>
+```
+
+The options available shall include:
+
+* `--limit` Runs the named command with CPU, memory, and disk IO limitations in place. (Default: true)
+* `--isolate` Runs the named command with isolated PID, mounts, and networking. (Default: true)
+
+It also required the `HERMIONE_SERVER` environment variable to be set to `host:port` of the Hermione service.
+
+This command will return immediately and output a job ID on the command-line. This job ID can be used to stop the process or query the status and output of the process.
+
+For example,
+
+```
+% hermione start /bin/ls -l /etc
+42
+% hermione status 42
+FINISHED (0)
+% hermione logs 42
+bashrc
+group
+hosts
+passwd
+```
+
+**Comments:**
+
+* _A complete implementation of this CLI should provide more flexibility in how it's run. Passing a file in describing details about how to run the command, limits, and isolation required, allowing the server to be passed in on the command-line, using environment variables in place of some command-line arguments, etc., all based on the needs of the operations staff or customers that will be running it._
+* _Here we can only control the command-line of the task being run. However, controlling the environment, input, making the TTY available, and other inputs are probably useful. These could be added._
+* _Control of limits and isolation are discussed further in later sections._
+
+#### Stop Command
+
+```shell
+hermione stop job-id
+```
+
+This command will block until the job is stopped or an internal timeout (length TBD). It will output the status of the process when the command stops.
+
+**Comments:**
+
+* _Configurable timeouts are handy. The POC provides no such configuration in the interest of time._
+
+#### Query Command
+
+```shell
+hermione status job-id
+```
+
+This command will return the current status of the command. The status will have one of four outputs. If the command could not be run, an error status will return with the internal error that caused the failure:
+
+```
+ERROR: reason for failure to start
+```
+
+The "reason for failure..." message will depend on the error that occurred. For example, if the command was not found, it might return:
+
+```
+ERROR: no such file or directory
+```
+
+The full list of possible diagnostic messages is TBD.
+
+The second possible status is `RUNNING`, which will return no additional information.
+
+The third possible status is `FINISHED` which will also return the exit code of process:
+
+```
+FINISHED (0)
+```
+
+The fourth possible status is `STOPPED` which shows the exit code like `FINISHED`, but shows that the command execution was interrupted by the user issuing a stop command.
+
+```
+STOPPED (1)
+```
+
+For finished and stopped status, an exit code of `0` will indicate successful completion of the process while a non-zero code indicates some sort of failure reported by the process itself.
+
+**Comments:**
+
+* _As nothing has been specified as to what "query status" means in the requirements, I am sticking to the simplest definition of status. However, it would be quite easy to expand status, particularly when `RUNNING` to include useful aspects like CPU usage, memory usage, list open files, network and disk I/O stats, or any number of other details. 
+* _This could even go so far as to include metrics and histograms of CPU load, memory usage, and so on, but I would generally delegate that to a telemetry system, such as prometheus metrics paired with Grafana or DataDog to make pretty dashboards, instead._
+
+### Command Output
+
+```shell
+hermione logs job-id
+```
+
+The options include:
+
+This returns the full output of the program, including both standard output and standard error streams combined.
+
+This command will block until eithe rhte user interrupts the local process (e.g., Ctrl-C) or the process begun vai the `start` command terminates (or immediately if already terminated).
+
+**Comments:**
+
+* _It would likely be useful to do something as simple as colorize the output based on which parts are standard error and which are standard out, but that has not been done in the interest of time._
+* _Making the output available as a JSON stream could also be useful, if the output needs to be processed into something else, such as a web UI._
+* _Options for showing only `--stdout` or `--stderr` would be helpful. We could even allow for additional log files to be tailed, depending on the needs of the tasks being run._
+
+### API
+
+The only aspects of this API that are provided are those necessary for supporting the command-line interface. I have broken up the protocol buffer definitions for the grpc by operation. As small as this API is, this will almost certainly be just a single file and single service containing all interface declarations.
+
+#### Start
+
+To run a task, you need to provide the command-line and you need to specify whether the resources of the command ought to be limited and/or isolated.
+
+```protobuf
+syntax = "proto3";
+
+message StartRequest {
+  // includes command and args
+  repeated string command_line = 1;
+  
+  // intended for debugging use only
+  bool prevent_limits = 2;
+  bool prevent_isolation = 3;
+}
+
+message StartResponse {
+  uint64 job_id = 1;
+}
+
+service Hermione {
+  rpc StartJob(StartRequest) returns (StartResponse);
+  // ...
+}
+```
+
+**Comments:**
+
+* _Discussion of why limits and isolation are optional is provided later in this document._
+
+#### Stop
+
+To stop a task, you need to provide a job-id to stop.
+
+```protobuf
+syntax = "proto3";
+
+message StopRequest {
+  uint64 job_id = 1;
+}
+
+enum JobStatus {
+  JOB_STATUS_ERROR = 0;
+  JOB_STATUS_RUNNING = 1;
+  JOB_STATUS_FINISHED = 2;
+  JOB_STATUS_STOPPED = 3;
+}
+
+message ProcessStatusInfo {
+  JobStatus status = 1;
+  uint64 exit_code = 2; // only meaningful when status == JOB_STATUS_FINISHED|JOB_STATUS_STOPPED
+  string error_message = 3; // only set when status == JOB_STATUS_ERROR
+}
+
+message StopResponse {
+  ProcessStatusInfo process_status = 1;
+}
+
+service Hermione {
+  rpc StopJob(StopRequest) returns (StopResponse);
+  // ...
+}
+```
+
+#### Status
+
+To check the status of a task, you need to provide a job-id to check.
+
+```protobuf
+syntax = "proto3";
+
+message StatusRequest {
+  uint64 job_id = 1;
+}
+
+// ProcessStatusInfo is shown with the Stop API above
+
+message StatusResponse {
+  ProcessStatusInfo process_status = 1;
+}
+
+service Hermione {
+  rpc QueryJob(StatusRequest) returns (StatusResponse);
+  // ...
+}
+```
+
+Though the `StatusRequest` and `StopRequest` messages are identical, they each get their own separate message definition. This allows for interface to be more resilient to potentially breaking changes. (That is, `StopRequest` and `StatusRequest`, should they evolve, are very likely to evolve differently from one another.)
+
+The `ProcessStatusInfo`, however, is shared because it serves the same purpose in both response objects.
+
+### Output
+
+Capturing output will be handled as a server-side stream. The input is just job ID again, but we also provide a flag allowing for following, if desired.
+
+```protobuf
+syntax = "proto3";
+
+enum OutputStream {
+   OUTPUT_STREAM_OUT = 1;
+   OUTPUT_STREAM_ERR = 2;
+}
+
+message OutputRequest {
+  uint64 job_id = 1;
+}
+
+message OutputResponse {
+  bytes chunk = 1;
+  OutputStream output_stream = 2; // never _BOTH
+}
+
+service Hermione {
+  rpc WatchJob(OutputRequest) returns (stream OutputResponse);
+  // ...
+}
+```
+
+The stream will remain open until either the client closes the connection (stops listening) or the task exits. All output is treated as binary and is unprocessed. The output and error streams may be returned separately. 
+
+### Library
+
+All business logic for Hermione will be placed inside packages within the `pkg/` folder of the project. This includes both the server-side and client-side code.
+
+THe project layout will generally follow [typical Golang practices](https://github.com/golang-standards/project-layout), including the following:
+
+* `.github/workflows` - I will place CI tools here to ensure that tests and linting is run for every PR. If time allows, this will also include a simple integration test.
+* `cmd/` - Go code related to the CLI. Code here is solely focused on parsing command-line arguments, environment, providing output, and calling business logic found in `pkg/`.
+* `docs/` - This file as well as an additional documentation files I need to create.
+* `pkg/` - Business logic for the project will be here, also tests.
+* `protos/` - I have generally opted for placing protobuf files in `protos/` rather than `api/`.
+* `tools/` - Any scripts, one-off code generators (probably won't be any for this project), and other tools will go here. This will at least include scripts for generating certificates for use with mTLS configuration and any special entrypoint scripts needed to ensure that cgroups and such work.
+
+The root directory will contain configuration for buf, linter, `main.go`, and other standard project files. The `README.md` will contain up-to-date instructions for installation and usage. This may also include a `Dockerfile` and a `docker-compose.yml` as my primary machine is an M2 Max and the easiest way to drop into a Linux environment is via Docker.
+
+**Comments:**
+
+* _Insofar as possible, business logic will be kept in either an `internal/` or `pkg/` folder following published golang best practice guidelines._ 
+* _For this POC, I will put all code in `pkg/`._
+
+#### Package Layout
+
+The final implementation may differ from this layout to some degree as I realize planning didn't take all the factors into account, but here's the plan:
+
+* `pkg/hermione/v1` - This will contain the automatically generated client and server stub code from the protocol buffers.
+* `pkg/auth` - This will contain the code for performing both authentication of mTLS for client and server as well as middleware for implementing the authorization scheme.
+* `pkg/config` - This will contain configuration used by the server to determine how to operate. If this weren't a POC, this would load the configuration from file (I usually prefer YAML), but in this case is completely hard coded.
+* `pkg/server` - This will include the code for running the service. In a more advanced server, this would include features like graceful shutdown, and configuration reload, but in this POC, no means of shutdown is provided aside from just interrupting the process.
+* `pkg/server/sdk` - This will contain the API implementation for each endpoint (i.e., code to fill in the server stubs generated by `protoc` in `pkg/hermione/v1`).
+* `pkg/task` - This will contain the code for running jobs, including code for setting up cgroups and user namespaces for isolation. A non-POC, might split these last two into a separate package or two.
+
+Going with typical Golang best practice, I've tried to select packages that are designed to group related aspects of code together. This is a balance between having too few packages, where unrelated aspects are grouped together, and having too many packages, where each aspect is completely isolated. Each aspect or feature should get its own source file within the package.
+
+#### Identifiers
+
+For the POC, monotonically incrementing serial numbers are used for job IDs. This is not necessarily ideal for certain reasons:
+
+1. A user can see how many commands have been run on a system. This could be a reputation risk if you want to make it seem like a server has been around a while (I've worked for an employer who would have cared about this risk, though not in this particular context).
+2. It makes IDs very guessable by an attacker. If credentials are compromised or if theres a security bug that grants some oracle when you know the ID, an attacker can use gain information or access they shouldn't have by guessing IDs. 
+
+The system should probably incorporate IDs that either some unguessable random elements, which can be gotten from ULID or UUID or SHA hashes of data, particularly if some random element is present.
+
+For simplicify, though, we'll stick to an auto-increment for IDs in he POC.
+
+#### Job Table
+
+The server will maintain an internal job table. This job table will contain a status structure like this:
+
+```golang
+type JobState int
+const (
+    JobStateError JobState = iota
+    StateRunning
+    JobStateFinished
+)
+    
+// JobInfo may have a different exact shape based 
+// on implementation, but should have something like 
+// all these fields.
+type JobInfo struct {
+    ID int
+    CommandLine []string
+    Status JobState
+    Err error
+    ExitCode int
+    OutputFile string
+}
+
+type JobTable map[int]JobInfo
+```
+
+A goroutine will be made responsible for managing the job table. The goroutine sleeps until queries are received via a Go channel. The calling process will send a job number and then the goroutine will return a copy of the job info for that job or an error back. It will have a second communication channel for handling writes, which accepts a command line and returns a job ID.
+
+All operations inside the goroutine are serial so theirs no risk of concurrency issues. The information reported back to the caller might be out of date by the time the caller receives it, but it should at least be very recently true.
+
+**Comments:**
+
+* _A mutex lock could be used, but should be avoided. Guarding critical sections with goroutines is nearly free of overhead because of the way they work and much easier to get right than locks._
+* _Only if profiling reveals that this goroutine is a bottleneck should alternatives to this sort of goroutine be considered, in my opinion. Even then, breaking the operation up or attempting to limit what it does to teh bare minimum might be better. Switching to atomic values or locks could be called for in some situations, but should be avoided. Not only do they contain hidden pitfalls, but seemingly unrelated changes can impact the operation of such things and concurrency errors created by race conditions and deadlocks are notoriously difficult to track down. Better to use something like a goroutine to carefully limit the risks._
+* _The job table is forgotten between runs. If we want better resiliency, it ought to be written to and read from a database of some kind rather than being held in memory. In that case, we may be able to eliminate the goroutine._
+
+#### Task Runners
+
+The job of the task runner will include:
+
+1. Run the program, with cgroups and namespaces setup as needed.
+2. Add the task to the [job table](#job-table).
+3. Ping any listening followers whenever output is written to standard output or standard error.
+4. Handle cleanup tasks when the process terminates:
+   * Set the error message in the job table on failure
+   * Set the exit code in the job table on completion
+   * Close the log file
+   * Clear up any other resource related to a running task (if any)
+   * Notify the notification goroutine one last time
+
+The writer that handles output to standard output and standard error for the job will write to the [output cache](#output-cache) whenever output from either of these streams is received.
+
+#### Output Cache
+
+The output cache keeps a file for each running task. This file tracks the output from that running task. This is not written as just a plain file because we want to keep the output and error streams separate, but interleaved similar to how they occur in the application.
+
+Each task has its own output cache, which writes to a file on disk. This file contains zero or more records of writes. Each record looks like this as a Go struct:
+
+```golang
+type OutputRecord struct {
+    Stream  byte   // 'E' for stderr, 'O' for stdout
+    Length  uint32 // Length == len(Chunk)
+    Chunk   []byte // data collecting from the running task
+	
+	// calculated value, not stored in the output cache file
+	Pointer uint64 // seek pointer to the start of the next record
+}
+```
+
+The fields are used as follows:
+* The `Stream` is a flag naming the stream. It only really needs to be a single bit, but bytes are simpler.
+* The `Length` encodes the number of bytes to read into `Chunk` when reading the record back from the file.
+* The `Chunk` is the data that was recieved from the running task.
+* The `Pointer` is not stored in the file, but 
+
+**Writes:** Each time output is received from the running task, a new `OutputRecord` is written to the cache file. The chunk is also sent to every listener via the [Notification Pub/Sub System](#notification-pub-sub-system).
+
+**Reads:** Listeners to the output of a task need to read from this output cache in two ways. First, they need to get all output that's already occurred replayed. Then, they need to get live updates. However, while replaying is being performed, new records may be written.
+
+A listener will synchronize the output using an operation like the following:
+
+```golang
+// ReplayRecords reads from the output cache file starting at the 
+// given file seek position
+func ReplayRecords(jobInfo *JobInfo, ptr uint64) <-chan OutputRecord {
+    ...
+}
+
+// ConsumeRecords subscribes to the notification pub/sub system for 
+// ongoing chunk notifications
+func ConsumeRecords(jobInfo *JobInfo) <-chan OutputRecord {
+    ...
+}
+
+// no error handling shown for brevity
+recPtr := uint64(0)
+for record := range ReplayRecords(jobInfo, recPtr) {
+    // replaying previous cached chunks
+    Send(record)
+    recPtr = record.Pointer
+}
+
+synced := false
+for record := range ConsumeRecords(jobInfo) {
+    if !synced && recPtr < record.Pointer {
+        for record := range ReplayRecords(recPtr) {
+            Send(record)
+            recPtr = record.Pointer
+        }
+        synced = true
+    }
+	
+    if recPtr < record.Pointer {
+        Send(record)
+        recPtr = record.Pointer
+    }
+}
+```
+
+The above assumes a regular file system and that writes to the cache file are flushed before the notification pub/sub system is sent any notifications. If this is writing to an NFS file system, e.g., flush might not mean much, and if flush is not being perrormed, the above syncrhonization scheme may skip some records. If the above algorithm proves insufficient, replacing the first `if` statement with a `for` loop that exits once `recPtr == record.Pointer`, should do the job. The second `if` condition should prevent any duplication of messages, though is not strictly necessary after the initial sync has been performed.
+
+This storage system has at least one **major** drawback: if we want to make it so that a user could specify logs since a given date or the last N lines, for example, it will require a lot of awkward seeking to make it work. It could be done, but finding the starting place would be a costly brute force operation.
+
+However, an external index making use of the `Pointer` values would be a reasonable solution and would allow for more random access into the file. The index could also include the number of lines in each chunk as well as record the timestamp of each chunk.
+
+**Comments:**
+
+* _The selection of a 4-byte `Length` is arbitrary. For streaming binary data, a 32KiB limit felt low and 8-bytes of length would be monster overkill. But I would not generally anticipate 4GiB chunks ever occurring. I'd want to monitor the behavior to study what chunks are normal once in production and see what, if anything, could be done here. It may be that my intuition is wrong and 32KiB is enough._
+* _The 0-value of the `Length` field will not be used. If a study of usage demonstrated that 4GiB chunks are possible, I would want to change this field to `LenghtMinusOne` to give us even 32-bit chunk sizes, but for simplicity of this POC and because I don't anticipate 4GiB chunks being encountered, we will keep it simple. (This is anothe reason to avoid uint32, because I can anticipate 32KiB chunks and I would feel like a  `LengthMinusOne` field is necessary in that case.)_
+* _For large logs, it is hypothetically possible that this could hit disk I/O limits for maximum file size on the file system. It may be desirable, therefore, in a hypothetical future release to expand the output cache to use multiple files. I leave this hypothetical improvement to a hypothetical programmer to implement in a hypothetical future._
+
+#### Notification Pub/Sub System
+
+This will manage communication of chunks received from running tasks as they are recieved live for those process that are listening for them. This is a goroutine that runs at all times. For the sake of hte POC, this will be a single goroutine, but could be broken down into more than one to improve throughput, if one goroutine turns out to be a bottleneck.
comment.body:
If the application is making routine writes of maximum size (0x7fff0000 IIRC) on Linux and the client is slow, yep, the POC is going to choke sending one user their data as currently planned.

All the solutions I can think of, though, will raise complexity or cause back pressure to slow down the task. The best solution I can think of would be to detect slow connections and shift them back into the catch up pool, replaying from file. That would keep them from applying back pressure that slows down all connections.

I suppose I could just keep all connections that way all the time and just have them play catch up from their own file handle instead of sending the bytes over the notification packets, which would eliminate the need for slow client detection.

@@ -0,0 +1,739 @@
+---
+authors: Sterling Hanenkamp (sterling@hanenkamp.com)
+state: draft
+---
+
+# RFD Z - Linux Job Worker Service Application (aka Hermione)
+
+## What
+
+Hermione is an MVP job worker service for running arbitrary Linux processes. This provides a service for running and managing zero or more processes on a machine (possibly remote), authenticating interactions, and a library and CLI for interacting with the service.
+
+## Why
+
+The primary goal of this service is to secure myself an offer from Teleport as part of the job interview process. This service should meet the requirements of their L5 challenge as that seems the most appropriate level representing my skill, career goals, and experience.
+
+Along the way, a secondary reason for performing this challenge is that it will introduce me to concepts with which I am familiar, but have not made direct use of in the past:
+
+* **cgroups** - I have generally taken these for granted when using containerization/orchestration tools such as Docker or Kubernetes, but have not made more direct use of in the past.
+* **mTLS** - I am very familiar with mutual authentication, but have not implemented such recently and never myself as part of a gRPC server.
+* **Linux Namespace Isolation** - This is another set of tools I'm aware of, but never used directly as I don't often make system calls or low-level use of `unshare` or similar tools. I usually use containerization tools for this.
+
+It is always good to continue expanding my skill set and experience as a means of keeping fresh with current technology and maintaining a flexible mind.
+
+### Naming
+
+Regarding the name, I've found "cutesy names" for projects make them more memorable. If this annoys the review panel, my apologies. There are reasons to avoid cutesy names sometimes, so maybe "JobRunner" would be a better name in some cases, but I am applying to Teleport, named after a project which is a cutesy name after all.
+
+ I have chosen the name "Hermione" (a Greek name often pronounced Her-My-Oh-Nee) for this proof of concept. In the Harry Potter books, her character spends much of her time trying to get her friends, Harry and Ron, to do their school work, so I feel it is a reasonably appropriate name. Besides, it's a fun name to say.
+
+## Details
+
+Through the remainder of this document, there are **Comments** sections added here and there to discuss trade-offs and future improvements that could be made were this not a one-off proof of concept (POC), but an application to be developed from MVP to production.
+
+### Approach
+
+#### Logical Direction
+
+My design is primarily top-down. I designed the CLI first, then considered the API that would be required to implement the CLI calls, and then finally how the library itself should be implemented in light of the needs of the API and CLI. As I've decided to make the CLI also run the service itself, some of the server-side aspects of the CLI were designed late (especially the `setup` sub-command).
+
+This design document presents the aspects of the design in this order: CLI, API, and Library with other details presented in their place.
+
+#### The Unknowns
+
+One important aspect of this project are the technologies with which I am unfamiliar. I had no direct knowledge of cgroups or Linux User Namespaces coming into the project. This is, in my experience, very typical.
+
+My solution to this lack of knowledge was to do follow this process, which is typical for me:
+
+1. Consume tutorials and encyclopedic documentation on the subject to get a feel for the landscape.
+2. Read the formal documentation of these features themselves.
+3. Find tools that use the features and use them myself to see how they work.
+4. Write a micro-sized proof of concept that implements these features in a one-off.
+
+The final step I did on my personal laptop which runs Pop_OS Linux (Ubuntu derivative). I wrote a three line counter program that counts upward every second and runs forever and then a second program that would place the counter program in a cgroup with limited resources and inside its own namespace using pure Go code. This 40-some line program is the basis for the implementation snippets shown later in this RFD.
+
+**Comments:**
+
+* _In a professional environment, I would expect to have a M3 Macbook Pro, which obviously is not running Linux. In that case, I will either use something like Docker or a VM to run Linux locally for this sort of task or spin up a tiny instance in whichever cloud provider the company uses to try things out as needed. Or use whatever infrastructure is already provided to devs for purpose, if it already exists._
+
+#### Design Principles
+
+Aside from logical ordering and process, I have taken the following principles into consideration:
+
+1. **Minimalism.** I've striven to implement only what is listed as a requirement. This challenge has very succinct and well-defined requirements, so this has been pretty easy.
+2. **Debuggability.** That is a made up word. There are some decisions made based on years of experience. For example, it is not necessary for limits and isolation to be optional, but it feels likely that making these optional will make debugging easier (e.g., is this weird error cropping up late in development because something is wrong with the process or because something is wrong with the cgroups configuration or implementation?)
+3. **Hubris.** The whole goal of this project is to demonstrate my capabilities, so hubris is necessarily implied. As a long time Perl-hacker, I'm proud to say that I've always striven to follow Larry Wall's Three Virtues: Laziness, Impatience, and Hubris. This project is especially focused on hubris.
+
+### Command-Line Interface
+
+The command-line interface implements both the client and server in a single service. I see no reason to create two separate commands when one can do both operations via sub-command. I have found that this is generally encouraged by the way Golang tools work anyway, so why fight it? If this is a problem, splitting them up requires very little effort, so that could be changed in the future two separate programs with about ten minutes extra work.
+
+The following sub-commands are provided:
+
+ * [`server setup`](#setup-server)
+ * [`server run`](#run-server)
+ * [`start`](#start-command)
+ * [`stop`](#stop-command)
+ * [`status`](#query-command)
+ * [`logs`](#command-output)
+
+#### Workflow
+
+Before describing each command in more detail. Let's consider the general workflow. To get started, the service must be running first. This can be done on an appropriate Linux machine, which could be the local machine. (Obviously, actual output once implemented may vary.)
+
+```
+% sudo hermione server setup
+% hermione server start
+Listening on :8443
+```
+
+That will get the service running. Then, tasks can be started, stopped, and checked using the other `hermione` commands:
+
+```
+% export HERMIONE_SERVER=127.0.0.1:8443
+% hermione start ls /
+1
+% hermione status 1
+FINISHED (0)
+% hermione server logs 1
+bin   dev   lib   libx32      mnt   recovery    sbin    sys   usr
+boot  etc   lib32 lost+found  opt   root        snap    tmp   var
+core  home  lib64 media       proc  run         srv
+```
+
+This represents a typical workflow. Multiple jobs may be run simultaneously and logs may be monitored live or after the fact.
+
+#### Setup Server
+
+The setup server command is run as follows:
+
+```shell
+sudo hermione server setup
+```
+
+This command performs one-time setup and checking that is required to enable the server to run properly. Mostly, this sets up the required permissions in the cgroup file system.
+
+This program will assume that the cgroup of the current parent process or shell will be the one that the `hermione` server will be using.
+
+#### Run Server
+
+The run server command is run as follows:
+
+```shell
+hermione server run
+```
+
+This will start the server on port `:8443` listening on all available interfaces. All aspects of the service configuration are hard coded. The server will run and block until killed.
+
+This service runs the gRPC API described under the [API](#api) section and traffic is encrypted and protected by mTLS authentication.
+
+**Comments:**
+
+* _It would be nice if the server provided tooling for starting, stopping, checking status, and asking it to reload configuration, but these have been left off of the POC in the interest of time._
+* _Reading configuration from external files would also be best in a complete production system._
+
+#### Start Command
+
+```shell
+hermione start [options] <command-line>
+```
+
+The options available shall include:
+
+* `--limit` Runs the named command with CPU, memory, and disk IO limitations in place.
+* `--isolate` Runs the named command with isolated PID, mounts, and networking.
+
+It also required the `HERMIONE_SERVER` environment variable to be set to `host:port` of the Hermione service.
+
+This command will return immediately and output a job ID on the command-line. This job ID can be used to stop the process or query the status and output of the process.
+
+For example,
+
+```
+% hermione start /bin/ls -l /etc
+42
+% hermione status 42
+FINISHED (0)
+% hermione logs 42
+bashrc
+group
+hosts
+passwd
+```
+
+**Comments:**
+
+* _A complete implementation of this CLI should provide more flexibility in how it's run. Passing a file in describing details about how to run the command, limits, and isolation required, allowing the server to be passed in on the command-line, using environment variables in place of some command-line arguments, etc., all based on the needs of the operations staff or customers that will be running it._
+* _Here we can only control the command-line of the task being run. However, controlling the environment, input, making the TTY available, and other inputs are probably useful. These could be added._
+* _Control of limits and isolation are discussed further in later sections._
+
+#### Stop Command
+
+```shell
+hermione stop job-id
+```
+
+This command will block until the job is stopped or an internal timeout (length TBD). It will output the status of the process when the command stops.
+
+**Comments:**
+
+* _Configurable timeouts are handy. The POC provides no such configuration in the interest of time._
+
+#### Query Command
+
+```shell
+hermione status job-id
+```
+
+This command will return the current status of the command. The status will have one of three formats. If the command could not be run, an error status will return with the internal error that caused the failure:
+
+```
+ERROR: reason for failure to start
+```
+
+The "reason for failure..." message will depend on the error that occurred. For example, if the command was not found, it might return:
+
+```
+ERROR: no such file or directory
+```
+
+The full list of possible diagnostic messages is TBD.
+
+The second possible status is `RUNNING`, which will return no additional information.
+
+The third possible status is `FINISHED` which will also return the exit code of process:
+
+```
+FINISHED (0)
+```
+
+Typically, an exit code of `0` will indicate successful completion of the process while a non-zero code indicates some sort of failure reported by the process itself.
+
+**Comments:**
+
+* _As nothing has been specified as to what "query status" means in the requirements, I am sticking to the simplest definition of status. However, it would be quite easy to expand status, particularly when `RUNNING` to include useful aspects like CPU usage, memory usage, list open files, network and disk I/O stats, or any number of other details. 
+* _This could even go so far as to include metrics and histograms of CPU load, memory usage, and so on, but I would generally delegate that to a telemetry system, such as prometheus metrics paired with Grafana or DataDog to make pretty dashboards, instead._
+
+### Command Output
+
+```shell
+hermione logs [options] job-id
+```
+
+The options include:
+
+* `--follow, -f` This will block until either the user interrupts the process (e.g., Ctrl-C) or the process begun via the `start` command terminates (or immediately if already terminated). This will output new lines of output from the process continuously as they become available.
+
+This returns the full output of the program, including both standard output and standard error streams combined.
+
+**Comments:**
+
+* _It would likely be useful to do something as simple as colorize the output based on which parts are standard error and which are standard out, but that has not been done in the interest of time._
+* _Making the output available as a JSON stream could also be useful, if the output needs to be processed into something else, such as a web UI._
+* _Options such as `--since` or `-n` for limiting the log by log messages since a given date or number of recent lines would be helpful, but not implemented for the sake of time._
+* _Options for showing only `--stdout` or `--stderr` would be helpful. We could even allow for additional log files to be tailed, depending on the needs of the tasks being run._

+### API
+
+The only aspects of this API that are provided are those necessary for supporting the command-line interface. I have broken up the protocol buffer definitions for the grpc by operation. As small as this API is, this will almost certainly be just a single file and single service containing all interface declarations.
+
+#### Start
+
+To run a task, you need to provide the command-line and you need to specify whether the resources of the command ought to be limited and/or isolated.
+
+```protobuf
+syntax = "proto3";
+
+message StartRequest {
+  repeated string command_line = 1;
+  bool limited = 2;
+  bool isolated = 3;
+}
+
+message StartResponse {
+  uint64 job_id = 1;
+}
+
+service Hermione {
+  rpc StartJob(StartRequest) returns (StartResponse);
+  // ...
+}
+```
+
+**Comments:**
+
+* _A more production-worthy implementation should probably deprecate the `limited` and `isolated` fields and add nested messages that allow for configuration of the limitations (percentage of CPU permitted, memory permitted, etc.) and isolation (how to limit PID, etc.)
+* _Discussion of why limits and isolation are optional is provided later in this document._
+
+#### Stop
+
+To stop a task, you need to provide a job-id to stop.
+
+```protobuf
+syntax = "proto3";
+
+message StopRequest {
+  uint64 job_id = 1;
+}
+
+enum JobStatus {
+  JOB_STATUS_ERROR = 0;
+  JOB_STATUS_RUNNING = 1;
+  JOB_STATUS_FINISHED = 2;
+}
+
+message ProcessStatusInfo {
+  JobStatus status = 1;
+  uint64 exit_code = 2; // only meaningful when status == JOB_STATUS_FINISHED
+  string error_message = 3; // only set when status == JOB_STATUS_ERROR
+}
+
+message StopResponse {
+  ProcessStatusInfo process_status = 1;
+}
+
+service Hermione {
+  rpc StopJob(StopRequest) returns (StopResponse);
+  // ...
+}
+```
+
+#### Status
+
+To check the status of a task, you need to provide a job-id to check.
+
+```protobuf
+syntax = "proto3";
+
+message StatusRequest {
+  uint64 job_id = 1;
+}
+
+// ProcessStatusInfo is shown with the Stop API above
+
+message StatusResponse {
+  ProcessStatusInfo process_status = 1;
+}
+
+service Hermione {
+  rpc QueryJob(StatusRequest) returns (StatusResponse);
+  // ...
+}
+```
+
+Though the `StatusRequest` and `StopRequest` messages are identical, they each get their own separate message definition. This allows for interface to be more resilient to potentially breaking changes. (That is, `StopRequest` and `StatusRequest`, should they evolve, are very likely to evolve differently from one another.)
+
+The `ProcessStatusInfo`, however, is shared because it serves the same purpose in both response objects.
+
+### Output
+
+Capturing output will be handled as a server-side stream. The input is just job ID again, but we also provide a flag allowing for following, if desired.
+
+```protobuf
+syntax = "proto3";
+
+message OutputRequest {
+  uint64 job_id = 1;
+  bool follow = 2;
+}
+
+message OutputResponse {
+  repeated string lines = 1;
+}
+
+service Hermione {
+  rpc WatchJob(OutputRequest) returns (stream OutputResponse);
+  // ...
+}
+```
+
+If the `follow` flag is set, the stream will remain open until either the client closes the connection (stops listening) or the task exits.
+
+**Comments:**
+
+* _I could have streamed a single line at a time. However, if I wanted to make it possible to stream multiple lines in the future, it could be a painful transition. If I want to always return a single in a `repeated` attribute, well, that's no so too annoying. However, I admit it might not be the best way to implement this._

+* `docs/` - This file as well as an additional documentation files I need to create.
+* `pkg/` - Business logic for the project will be here, also tests.
+* `protos/` - I have generally opted for placing protobuf files in `protos/` rather than `api/`.

This may also include a `Dockerfile` and a `docker-compose.yml` as my primary machine is an M2 Max and the easiest way to drop into a Linux environment is via Docker.
+
+**Comments:**

+* _Insofar as possible, business logic will be kept in either an `internal/` or `pkg/` folder following published golang best practice guidelines._

+#### Package Layout
+
+The final implementation may differ from this layout to some degree as I realize planning didn't take all the factors into account, but here's the plan:
+
+* `pkg/hermione/v1` - This will contain the automatically generated client and server stub code from the protocol buffers.
+* `pkg/auth` - This will contain the code for performing both authentication of mTLS for client and server as well as middleware for implementing the authorization scheme.
+* `pkg/config` - This will contain configuration used by the server to determine how to operate. If this weren't a POC, this would load the configuration from file (I usually prefer YAML), but in this case is completely hard coded.
+* `pkg/server` - This will include the code for running the service. In a more advanced server, this would include features like graceful shutdown, and configuration reload, but in this POC, no means of shutdown is provided aside from just interrupting the process.
+* `pkg/server/sdk` - This will contain the API implementation for each endpoint (i.e., code to fill in the server stubs generated by `protoc` in `pkg/hermione/v1`).
+* `pkg/task` - This will contain the code for running jobs, including code for setting up cgroups and user namespaces for isolation. A non-POC, might split these last two into a separate package or two.

+Going with typical Golang best practice, I've tried to select packages that are designed to group related aspects of code together. This is a balance between having too few packages, where unrelated aspects are grouped together, and having too many packages, where each aspect is completely isolated. Each aspect or feature should get its own source file within the package.

+#### Job Table
+
+The server will maintain an internal job table. This job table will contain a status structure like this:
+
+```golang
+type JobState int
+const (
+    JobStateError JobState = iota
+    StateRunning
+    JobStateFinished
+)
+    
+// JobInfo may have a different exact shape based 
+// on implementation, but should have something like 
+// all these fields.
+type JobInfo struct {
+    ID int
+    CommandLine []string
+    Status JobState
+    Err error
+    ExitCode int
+    OutputFile string
+}
+
+type JobTable map[int]JobInfo
+```
+
+A goroutine will be made responsible for managing the job table. The goroutine sleeps until queries are received via a Go channel. The calling process will send a job number and then the goroutine will return a copy of the job info for that job or an error back. It will have a second communication channel for handling writes, which accepts a command line and returns a job ID.
+
+All operations inside the goroutine are serial so theirs no risk of concurrency issues. The information reported back to the caller might be out of date by the time the caller receives it, but it should at least be very recently true.
+
+**Comments:**
+
+* _A mutex lock could be used, but should be avoided. Guarding critical sections with goroutines is nearly free of overhead because of the way they work and much easier to get right than locks._
+* _Only if profiling reveals that this goroutine is a bottleneck should alternatives to this sort of goroutine be considered, in my opinion. Even then, breaking the operation up or attempting to limit what it does to teh bare minimum might be better. Switching to atomic values or locks could be called for in some situations, but should be avoided. Not only do they contain hidden pitfalls, but seemingly unrelated changes can impact the operation of such things and concurrency errors created by race conditions and deadlocks are notoriously difficult to track down. Better to use something like a goroutine to carefully limit the risks._
+* _The job table is forgotten between runs. If we want better resiliency, it ought to be written to and read from a database of some kind rather than being held in memory. In that case, we may be able to eliminate the goroutine._
+
+#### Task Runners
+
+The job of the task runner will include:
+
+1. Run the program, with cgroups and namespaces setup as needed.
+2. Add the task to the [job table](#job-table).
+3. Ping any listening followers whenever output is written to standard output or standard error.
+4. Handle cleanup tasks when the process terminates:
+   * Set the error message in the job table on failure
+   * Set the exit code in the job table on completion
+   * Close the log file
+   * Clear up any other resource related to a running task (if any)
+   * Notify the notification goroutine one last time
+
+The writer that handles output to standard output or error for the job will send a notification to the [Notification Pub/Sub System](#notification-pub-sub-system) that notifies listeners of new output to consume.
+
+#### Streaming Output
+
+Just a quick note about streaming output. For the sake of the POC, the output will be written into temporary files, one per task started. The index of these files is handled by the [Job Table](#job-table).
+
+Each time the API is queried for logs, the gRPC server will have a separate thread for that response. That API response will first register itself with a notification goroutine. It will query the job table for the name of the log file and then open that file. It will read all the data available in that file using a line buffer, record the number of bytes read, and then close the file (leaving some bytes potentially unread because they haven't been terminated). The handler will now go to sleep.
+
+For the sake of the POC, I am assuming all output is line-based and will use line buffering for the streams.
+
+It will wake again whenever a notification is received from the notification goroutine. This can happen either because more input was received from the job or because the job has terminated. In either case, we repeat the process of the previous paragraph, except that we seek to the last byte already read first.
+
+At any point, if the job descriptor shows that the job is no longer in running state, the stream will exit after it finishes reading.
+When the stream exits, it sends a notification to the notifier goroutine that it is no longer interested in updates. 
+
+There should be little to no risk of race conditions or deadlocks in this system. The critical part will be the notification system.
+
+**Comments:**
+
+* _If this is to be used with tasks that have binary output, the way output is monitored will have to change to send chunks instead of lines. If used with something like a JSON log stream that doesn't emit line breaks, a change will also need to be made to figure out how to determine appropriate chunk breaks (though, the solution for binary output should work as a general solution). I have assumed line-based output._
+* _If resource contention were to become a problem, we should store the output in an external database that can be queried instead. We could do something complicated like having a shared pool of file handles we seek around in, but why? Just using redis or some other database to handle the data would be considerably more sensible._
+
+#### Notification Pub/Sub System
+
+There will be a bridge between the [task runner](#task-runners) and the [log stream routines](#streaming-output). This will be a goroutine that runs at all times. For the sake of hte POC, this will be a single goroutine, but could be broken down into more than one to improve throughput, if one goroutine turns out to be a bottleneck.
+
+It will need to receive two kinds of messages. It will, in some cases, send a message to one or more recipients.
+
+1. **Register Listener.** 
+   * Whenever a logs stream task is started with the `follow` flag set, that stream will send a registration message. 
+   * That message will consist of a `chan<- struct{}` channel and a job ID. 
+   * The notification goroutine maintains a map of job IDs to slices of channels. 
+   * The notification system will check the [job table](#job-table) to see if the job is currently running during registration. If the job is not running, the channel will immediately be sent one notification and will not be registered for further messages (which will never come). We send the one message to make sure the log stream has a chance to close itself down as well.
+2. **Job Update.** 
+   * Whenever a task log is written or the task is terminated, a message is sent that includes the job ID and a flag indicating whether the job is running or not. 
+   * This will cause the notifier to lookup all the channels registered for that job ID. It will send an empty struct to each registered listener. 
+   * If the job is no longer running, the notifier will also remove all channels from that job ID in the registration map.
+   * If one of the registered listeners fails to receive because the channel is closed, it will be removed from the registration list.
+
+It is possible if a task doesn't have much output, but runs a long time and there are a lot of listeners with the follow flag set that start and stop, that there could be a large number of a close channels in the registration list. For the POC, nothing is done to avoid this problem. However, it could be wise to send a "keep alive" ping to all listeners periodically to detect these and clear them out to free up resources. This would wake up each listener unnecessary from time to time, but shouldn't hurt anything otherwise.
+
+#### Regarding Goroutine
+
+Just a quick note regarding the interaction with goroutines. I will provide library function calls for interacting with the goroutines that at least partially hide the implementation. Most code won't know that communication with a goroutine is happening via channels. This way, if a later implementation moves some aspect from a goroutine to something, the calls don't need to change, just the implementation.
+
+For example, instead of using a goroutine for handling file update notifications, we might want to share information across replicas and use a message queue instead. Having to update the log stream code to work with a message queue rather than a channel should not be necessary. Instead, we'll just change the notification system to provide an unchanging interface in either case. At least, that's the theory.

+#### Cgroups
+
+The implementation of cgroups will use cgroup v2. The expected setup of cgroups for the service will be as follows. The server will assume the cgroup file system is mounted to `/sys/fs/cgroup` and that the current cgroup can be found by reading `/proc/self/cgroup`. We will also assume the system has the `cpu`, `memory`, and `io` controllers enabled for the system. (As Go 1.22 tests make these assumptions, I feel pretty safe with them.)
+
+Before the `hermione server run` command can be run (at least, if the limits are to be applied), the `sudo hermione server setup` command must be run. This requires root-level permissions to enable certain operations. Essentially, this works something like the following:
+
+```golang
+myCgroup := extractGroup("/proc/self/cgroup") // pulls the current cgroup from proc
+myCgparts := strings.Split(myCgroup, "/")
+current := "/sys/fs/cgroup" // /proc/self/cgroup does not include the mount point
+
+// this is a do..until loop, guaranteed to terminate because myCgparts cannot
+// have infinite length: grant each subtree control over the controllers
+// we need
+for {
+    stcPath := filepath.Join(current, "cgroup.subtree_control")
+    stcFile, err := os.OpenFile(stcPath, os.O_APPEND|os.O_WRONLY, 0)
+    if err != nil {
+        // handle err
+    } 
+
+    // As of this writing, I've only tested this piece using echo and shell 
+    // commands, so...
+	
+    // TODO Determine if a sync or something is required here. I believe each 
+    // has to be implemented via a separate system-level write. Might be better 
+    // to use syscalls for that reason.
+    stcFile.WriteString("+cpu\n")
+    stcFile.WriteString("+memory\n")
+    stcFile.WriteString("io\n")
+
+    if len(myCgparts) == 0 {
+		break
+    }
+
+    current := filepath.Join(current, myCgparts[0])
+    myCgparts := myCgparts[1:]
+}
+```
+
+The `setup` command will also do some basic sanity checking to help diagnose problems with cgroup configuration (more as a debugging aid for the POC than a feature).
+
+At startup, the `hermione server run` command will do some preparatory work like the following:
+
+```golang
+myCgroup := extractGroup("/proc/self/cgroup") // pulls the current cgroup from proc
+cgroupOrigin := filepath.Join("/sys/fs/cgroup", myCgroup)
+cgroupHome, err := os.MkdirTemp(cgroupOrigin, "hermione-task-manager-")
+if err != nil {
+    // handle err
+}
+```
+
+From there, each limited task will run something like this to start the process, assuming the `cgroupHome` variable is the one calculated above:
+
+```golang
+taskCgroup, err := os.MkdirTemp(cgroupHome, "subtask-")
+if err != nil {
+    // handle err
+}
+
+// actual hard-coded limits may be different, TBD
+setCpuMax(taskCgroup, 0.2) // writes "200000 1000000" to cpu.max
+setMemMax(taskCgroup, 1 * Gigabyte) // writes "1073741824" to memory.max
+
+// next bit writes "$maj:$min rbps=1048576 wpbs=2097152" to io.max
+maj, min := lookupRootDevice() // find device numbers for the / mount
+setIoMax(taskCgroup, maj, min, 1*Megabyte, 2*Megabyte)
+
+fd := getCgroupFD(taskCgroup)
+cmd := exec.Command(cmdLine...)
+// other setup...
+cmd.SysProcAttr = &syscall.SysProcAttr{
+    UseCgroupFD: true,
+    CgroupFD:    fd,
+}
+
+err := cmd.Run()
+if err != nil {
+    // handle err
+}
+```
+
+For the POC, this implementation will stick to hard-coded limits. These will at least be recorded in the hard-coded configuration, though, so it would be fairly easy to make these limits configurable globally. After the program completes running, we will ensure that the cgroup is torn down by removing the directory, if necessary.
+
+#### Namespace Isolation
+
+Namespace isolation will be implemented by setting flags during command execution within the Golang standard library. This is done by setting the following flags on the `syscall.SysProcAttr` part of the `exec.Command` struct:
+
+```golang
+cmd.SysProcAttr = &syscall.SysProcAttr{ 
+	Credential:  &syscall.Credential{
+        Uid: uint32(uid),
+        Gid: uint32(gid),
+    },
+    UidMappings: []syscall.SysProcIDMap{
+        { ContainerID: uid, HostID: uid, Size: 1 },
+    },
+    GidMappings: []syscall.SysProcIDMap{
+        { ContainerID: gid, HostID: gid, Size: 1 },
+    }
+    Cloneflags: syscall.CLONE_NEWNS |
+                syscall.CLONE_NEWNET |
+                syscall.CLONE_NEWPID |
+                syscall.CLONE_NEWUSER,
+}
+```
+
+Rather than repeat myself, you can imagine the setting of `SysProcAttr` being merged into the code shown under [Cgroups](#cgroups) for how processes are started there with limits.
+
+With the shown flags set, Golang will clone the child process into the new namespaces for PID, mounts, and network during fork (or, I believe, it will call `clone3` directly in this case).
+
+This will also clone the user and map the current user into the namespace. This is required because I intend for the Hermione service to run unprivileged.
+
+NOTE: I am basing the `CLONE_NEWUSER` implementation details more on practice with my test environment than real knowledge at this point. I believe this is a good POC solution in my aim to get to a working tool in a short time period. For production, I definitely want to spend more time learning about the permissions model for namespaces and ensure that I work with them in the best possible way.

+

+

+#### In-Scope: Linux System Setup
+
+I will need to specify the basic Linux configuration necessary to make this system works, as it depends on some fairly specific features of Linux. Scripts will be provided in the `tools/` folder to ensure proper startup of the service. Ideally, I will incorporate these into an integration test that runs as part of the CI tasks in GitHub Actions.
+
+I will be using cgroup v2 to implement this system.
+
+I have added the `hermione server setup` command to aid implement this aspect of the solution. I may also provide a `Dockerfile` or other tools to help ensure a Linux environment is provided to meet the needs of the service.
+
+#### Out-of-Scope: Separating the Control Plane from the Data Plane
+
+I have implemented this as a pretty vanilla client-server solution. If this weren't a POC, I would likely prefer to break the server into two parts, using terminology adopted from the service mesh industry: a control plane and a data plane. The control plane would be responsible for tracking, gathering telemetry, providing the API, message queueing, and other centralized concerns. The data plane would then be responsible for running jobs, generating telemetry and logging, interacting with and supervising the workload, and collecting output and assets from the job.
+
+The reason for a split design is that such a system is far more flexible. For example, if the requirements were expanded to make it possible to run jobs across multiple nodes or with high availability, it is considerably easier to do so with this split in place.
+
+Obviously, all of that is beyond the scope of this POC.
+
+#### Out-of-Scope: Telemetry
+
+On a project of this type, I would usually include a variety of telemetry tools, such as prometheus metrics, logging, and perhaps a database and/or queue of some kind for tracking job operation. I have placed such concerns out of scope. Some amount of local on-disk or console logging will be used for the sake of aiding debugging during development, but that is all.
+
+#### In-Scope: Optional Limits and Isolation
+
+The requirements do not specifically mention being able to select whether limits and isolation are applied. However, I have chosen to make these configurable at runtime because I anticipate it will be easier for me when doing manual testing to debug problems as the increased complexity of applying cgroups and namespace isolation separately will allow me to be more systematic.
+
+### Security
+
+#### Authentication
+
+Authentication will be performed based on whether the client-side and server-side certificates belong to the expected Certificate Authority. For the sake of simplicity, we will use a self-signed CA. A production system should make use of a well-known CA instead.
+
+I will provide simple scripts using `openssl` to generate the certificates. These will be based on 2048-bit RSA or a 256-bit ECDSA keys (TBD) for the private certificates. These certificates will be in hardcoded locations and mostly be named `server.pem` and `client.pem` and expect to be present in the working directory when the command-line program is run. A post-POC solution should make this part of a complete configuration system maybe something similar to the `kubectl` configuration directory, which includes certs for Kubernetes logins with a central configuration file to allow the caller to have multiple identities as necessary.
+
+I will be assuming that the `grpc` and Go standard libraries for configuring TLS and PK configuration in Golang operates according to industry best practices for setting up the TLS layer during client connections. I suspect, but cannot prove, this is a pretty safe assumption. Before moving into production, someone knowledgeable in TLS encryption should verify that the TLS configuration is secure. If not, we should be able to use a proxy server (e.g., nginx or Envoy) to implement the TLS in a more secure fashion according to current best practices. I risk being overly cautious to the point of paranoia, though, in saying all of this.
+
+#### Authorization
+
+No authorization is performed by the client. It only cares that the server is authentic. A future implementation could use HSTS to ensure this identity with a high level of certainty, if that's a concern. (I don't anticipate that this system would require authorization of the server and any such authorization could probably be solved on the server side.)
+
+Authorization of clients by the server will be provided by a simplistic means. The client-side certificate will include a `CN` and `O` definition. We will use the organization (`O` part) of the certificate name to determine whether the user has just read permissions (access to query status and see output) or read-write permissions (read permissions plus access to start and stop tasks). No other levels or abstraction will be provided.
+
+One `O` (name TBD) will have read-and-write-type permission. All others will just have read-type permissions.
